awd_titl_txt: EA: Upgrade to X-ray Diffraction Multiuser Facility for Earth and Environmental Science and Student Training
awd_abstract_narration:
This project will upgrade an aging X-ray diffractometer at the University of Georgia (UGA). X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a key method used to identify minerals, especially in materials that are too small to see with the naked eye. The UGA Department of Geology has operated an XRD facility for many years. The departments of Chemistry, Pharmacy, Food Sciences, Marine Sciences, Engineering, and others also use this resource. The facility assists the local community by identifying minerals and solving industrial problems. These uses align with the goal of the National Science Foundation (NSF) to support science, health, and well-being.

The upgrade will enhance the Bruker D8 diffractometer, which was first purchased in 2010 with funds from NSF. This instrument has contributed to over 100 research papers, two books, and has helped in the training and education of more than 500 students. The upgrade will allow the XRD facility to continue supporting research and student training. Several projects will use the upgraded diffractometer, covering Critical Minerals, Energy Generation, Environmental Stewardship, Resource Storage, and Geohealth. Some examples of these projects include: 1) Curation of the Allard Economic Geology Collection – a collection of minerals that’s part of one of the largest natural history collections in the U.S. 2) Critical Zone Science studies – which look at erosion caused by human activities and how microbes affect soil, from the treetops to the bedrock. 3) Research on PFAS (Forever Chemicals) – studying how these chemicals behave underground and interact with soil minerals. 4) Critical Minerals studies – focusing on materials essential for energy technologies that might be in danger of supply shortages. XRD is crucial for identifying these minerals, especially in the Southeastern U.S., where some clay mine wastes contain rare earth elements.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This grant supported the repair and modernization of the X-ray diffraction (XRD) facility in the Department of Geology at the University of Georgia (UGA). Funds were used to replace a defective X-ray tube tower that had logged more than 70,000 hours of operation. Bruker service technicians completed the repair, restoring the instrument to full functionality.

Since the repair, the instrument has been in nearly continuous use for instruction, research, and outreach, logging more than 4,000 hours during its first six months of operation. The XRD facility supported a graduate-level clay mineralogy course with 18 students, who received hands-on training in both the theory and practice of X-ray diffraction. The class also competed in the international Reynolds Cup competition using XRD data, providing an outstanding example of experiential learning.

The facility supported research by approximately 20 graduate students and seven undergraduate students. Most of the undergraduate researchers presented their findings at the UGA Center for Undergraduate Research Opportunities Symposium, an event that attracts more than 800 participants (see photos). The XRD facility also continues to support peer-reviewed research conducted by graduate students and faculty across multiple disciplines, including Engineering, Food Science, Chemistry, Textiles, and Ecology. In addition, the instrument is being used for collaborative projects with industry partners to solve problems related to material properties.

The XRD facility is now a key component of academic research on critical minerals, including projects funded by the U.S. Department of Energy to characterize mine wastes along the eastern seaboard of the United States and evaluate their potential as rare earth element resources.

The upgraded XRD facility has also contributed substantially to the broader impacts of this award by strenghtening the creation of the international Growing Partnerships for Essential Minerals (GEMs) workshop series (https://gems.research.gatech.edu/). This initiative has established a network of academic, industry, and government partners focused on developing sustainable critical mineral supply chains. As an essential tool for characterizing mineral ores, co-produced waste streams, and mineral processing products needed to meet growing demand for rare earth elements and other critical minerals, the XRD facility serves as a foundational research infrastructure.

Equally important, the facility is helping train the next generation of geoscientists and engineers with the technical expertise needed to develop efficient, sustainable approaches for recovering critical minerals from existing mining operations. This workforce development supports the production of materials essential for advanced technologies while contributing to the economic resilience and resource security of the United States and its international partners.
